title: Be strong (Joshua 1:1–9)
hook: Moses' successor is told three times, "be strong and of good courage"

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nevi'im, the Prophets, opening on the day Moses dies. Your line was the story goes on without moses. Did you notice something you're carrying on for someone? Today, the first words Joshua hears. Day six hundred ninety-eight.

What do you say to someone on the first morning of a job far too big for them? Joshua has just stepped into Moses' place. Until yesterday he was Moses' assistant; the book's first verse calls him Moses' minister. Now there's a river in front of him, a land of walled cities beyond it, and a whole people looking at him to see what happens next. God speaks. There's a promise of the land, border to border, but no battle plan, no tactics, no word about the walls. There's one phrase, said, then said again, then said a third time. And before the chapter ends, someone says it back to him.
screen: `A JOB TOO BIG.` → `NO BATTLE PLAN.` → `ONE PHRASE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Read Joshua chapter one and listen for the repeat. First: be strong and of good courage, because you will lead this people into the land. That one is about the task. Then again, stronger: only be strong and very courageous. And this time the reason is a surprise. Not to fight. To keep the teaching Moses gave, without turning from it to the right or to the left. Then the line: "This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth, but thou shalt meditate therein day and night." The bravest thing asked of the new leader isn't a battle. It's to keep studying, to keep the words in his mouth. Then a third time, with a third reason: be strong and of good courage, don't be afraid, don't be dismayed, "for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest." So: the work, the teaching, and company. Now skip to the end of the chapter. Joshua gives his first orders, and the tribes whose land lies east of the Jordan answer him. Whatever you command, we'll do. Wherever you send us, we'll go. And they close with the very words he was given: only be strong and of good courage. The encouragement that came down to Joshua goes back up to him from the people. Notice what kind of thing courage is here. It isn't a mood you wait for. It's a command. It can be spoken, repeated, and handed on, from God to a leader, and from a crowd to the person in front of it.
screen: `FIRST: FOR THE TASK.` · `SECOND: FOR THE TEACHING, DAY AND NIGHT.` · `THIRD: GOD IS WITH YOU.` · then, large: `THE PEOPLE SAY IT BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: encourage yourself out loud. Bring to mind one thing this week that feels too big. Name it, quietly. Then say, aloud if you can, or in a low voice if you're not alone: be strong. Say it once for the task itself. Say it again for whatever you're trying to stay faithful to while you do it. Say it a third time for the people who are with you in it. If you pray, you can add the verse's last words: the Lord thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest. Then sit, and let the words settle. The bell holds the time.
Be strong. Chazak, in Hebrew, said to Joshua three times, and then said back to him by the people. Today's word.
Your line: be strong, again. Today, say be strong to someone who's starting something hard, the way the tribes said it to Joshua. Day six hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: The words chazak ve'ematz, be strong and of good courage, come from Joshua 1, and some say the phrase to encourage someone taking on a new task.

match.prompt: be strong, three times — tap the pairs.
pairs: you will lead the people into the land
to keep the teaching, day and night
God is with you wherever you go

myth: God tells Joshua to be strong only for the battles ahead
the second time, the reason is the teaching: meditate therein day and night.
the people say be strong back to Joshua
at the end of chapter one the tribes answer: only be strong and of good courage.
Joshua is given a battle plan in chapter one
no tactics: a promise of the land, a book to keep in his mouth, and be strong.

fork.setup: you're one of the tribes. Joshua, the new leader, has just given his first orders. how do you answer him?
options: wait and see if he's as good as Moses.
promise to follow, and tell him to be strong.
ask for Moses' plans in writing first.
fork.reveal: they promise to go wherever he sends them, and end with the words he was just given: only be strong and of good courage.

original.note: Hebrew: be strong and of good courage, the phrase of Joshua 1.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pep talk before a war.
what it means: be strong, said three times with three reasons, the land, the teaching and God's company, and then said back by the people.
what a scholar hears: the strongest form, very courageous, is tied not to battle but to keeping the Torah in your mouth day and night.

notes: Verify exact JPS 1917 wording of Joshua 1:8 and the end of 1:9.
'Three times' counts God's charge in 1:6, 1:7 and 1:9; the people's echo is 1:18. Confirm the count and that 1:7 reads 'strong and very courageous'.
Day 696 already tied chazak to the end-of-book custom; this day stays in the text of Joshua 1 to avoid repeating it.
howItsDone: the custom of saying chazak ve'ematz to someone taking office is described loosely; a Keeper may refine or cut it.

Editor: cut 'the one standing near the tent' (not in Joshua 1) for 'Moses' minister' (1:1); 'again, louder' became 'again, stronger'; the answering tribes named as those east of the Jordan (1:12–18); howItsDone custom softened to 'some say'.
Audit: 'no map' was wrong, since Joshua 1:3–4 sets out the land's borders; hook, screen and myth now say no battle plan or tactics, and name the promise of the land.
